items.title: Ron Carter — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: he could have called Wilbur Ware, he could have called Sam, he could have called other guys.

ctx.x: You've used the phrase that this was a milestone moment for you, but I would like to understand why and how so.

Well then, you know, he'd made records with other bass players: Sam and probably Percy. I never played with Hank Jones. I hadn't met Hank Jones before and didn't know Ray Baretto. I think I met Lex Humphries somewhere. But they're all strangers. And I know Orrin Keepnews had his cadre of musicians he always hired. I understood that. They know Orrin, they've got a budget worked out with the personalities, they know … they just had such a … a fit for them. But for me to walk in to this slot that used to be taken up…

You started to mention some of the older bass players that could have been called and I'm wondering, in your still relatively early years, did any of the older bass players take you under their wing, did anybody act as mentor in any way? I'm thinking of people like Milt or …

items.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview
items.q: ut Richard Davis says that he practices -- or Ron Carter, for instance, says that he practices an awful lot.

ctx.x: That's true, that's true. Like it's hard for me to play the same thing twice exactly alike. It's hard to do because I never studied that way. I've never really studied or practiced like you see some people get up and practice, half the day, half the night, and when I practice, I'm practicing while I'm working.
But Richard Davis says that he practices -- or Ron Carter, for instance, says that he practices an awful lot.
Yeah, well, those kind of cats do. I remember Richard in Chicago, way before he left, I first met him. He invited me over to his house and he had the books be-
